evidence.label: Critical bond and site percolation on the cubic lattice
No percolation at criticality on quasi-transitive graphs

headline: At the exact tipping point, random networks of a broad, symmetric kind form no endless cluster.
scope: The general result covers bond percolation on infinite, connected, quasi-transitive graphs with finite links per point and p_c below 1.
plain: Open each link of a network at random with the same chance. Above a critical chance, an endless connected cluster appears. These papers prove that exactly at the critical chance, no endless cluster exists. One paper proves this for links and for points on the three-dimensional grid. The other proves it for links on every graph in the broad family Benjamini and Schramm named in 1996.
doesNot: This does not find any graph's critical chance, or settle site percolation beyond the cubic grid.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: Itai Benjamini and Oded Schramm, the criticality conjecture
scorecard.significanceWhy: If the proof holds, it settles the bond form of a central 30-year-old conjecture in percolation.

explanation:
Picture an endless square grid of streets. Flip a fair coin for every block of street. Heads keeps the block open, tails closes it. A corner has four blocks, so it is cut off with chance 1/16. A fixed route of 20 blocks is fully open with chance 1 in 1,048,576. But routes are many. From one corner, 4,649,045,868 routes of 20 blocks never turn straight back. That count is over 4,000 times the odds against any single route.

This game is called bond percolation. Each link of a network is open with some chance p, independently of the others. A cluster is a group of points joined by open links. For small p, every cluster is finite. For p near 1, an endless cluster appears. The switch point is the critical probability, written p_c. On the square grid, Harry Kesten showed in 1980 that p_c equals 1/2.

The hard question is what happens exactly at p_c. Does an endless cluster already exist there, or only just above it? If none exists, the chance of joining an endless cluster starts at zero and rises without a jump. For the square grid, work by Harris in 1960 and Kesten in 1980 settled the question. Hara and Slade handled grids of high enough dimension in 1990. In 2017, Fitzner and van der Hofstad covered dimension 11 and up. The planar methods do not work for paths in three dimensions.

In 1996, Itai Benjamini and Oded Schramm asked the question far more widely. Their conjecture covers every quasi-transitive graph with p_c below 1. A graph is quasi-transitive if its points come in finitely many types. Any two points of one type can be swapped by a symmetry of the whole graph. Every grid qualifies. Earlier work settled large families. In 2016, Tom Hutchcroft covered every such graph of exponential growth. That means the number of points within distance r grows like a fixed number raised to the power r. What remained was slower growth.

The first paper treats the cubic grid, in three dimensions. It proves that critical bond percolation there has no endless cluster. The same holds for site percolation, where the points rather than the links are open or closed. This was not untouched ground. In August 2026, Justin Leder publicly reported a Lean formalization of the bond case. It covers every grid of dimension 2 or more. Public expositions written by AI systems, prompted by Ahmed Bou-Rabee, reported the site case from dimension 3 up. The paper credits these and aims to give its own self-contained argument.

The second paper proves the full bond form of the Benjamini–Schramm conjecture. Take any infinite, connected graph where each point has finitely many links. Suppose it is quasi-transitive and its p_c is below 1. Then at p_c, there is almost surely no endless open cluster. Almost surely means with probability exactly one. The condition on p_c matters. A single endless line has p_c equal to 1, and at chance 1 every link is open.

The obstacle was the middle ground of growth. Graphs that grow slower than exponentially need not look like flat grids. The paper splits them into two kinds. Count the points within distance r of a point. In one kind, that count outgrows every fixed power of r. In the other, it sometimes grows no faster than a fixed power, much like a grid. For that kind, a known structure theorem by Tessera and Tointon supplies grid-like coordinates. In the grid-like case, the argument runs by contradiction. An endless cluster at p_c would force one slightly below p_c. The definition of p_c rules that out.

Return to the street grid, now in three dimensions. Set each block open with exactly the critical chance. Then every corner almost surely sits in a finite cluster. The results do not say what p_c is for the cubic grid. The general theorem covers bond percolation only. The paper notes that it does not imply the site version, which it proves separately only for the cubic grid.

How sure is this? A computer proof checker called Lean has a formal proof of each main statement. One covers bond and site percolation on the cubic grid. The other covers bond percolation on every graph described above, and allows repeated links between two points. Each is matched against a fixed reference statement by a tool called Comparator. No specialist review of either paper has been published.
hypeCheck: Lean proofs of both main statements are listed, with Comparator reference statements. The cubic bond case was already reported in public by others in 2026. No specialist review of either paper has been published.

glossary.meaning: A random network where each link is open with the same chance, independently of the others.
The same game played with points instead of links: each point is open or closed at random.
A group of points joined to each other by open links.
The chance p_c at which an endless cluster first becomes possible.
A network whose points come in finitely many types, each type looking the same everywhere.
When the number of points within distance r grows like a fixed number raised to the power r.
